literal: Cha had the censorate memorialize against him; he was summoned by post to the capital.
idiomatic: Cha prompted the censorate to impeach him; couriers summoned him to the capital.

literal: On review there was no substance.
idiomatic: Review found no case.

literal: He returned to his post and died.
idiomatic: He resumed his post and died.

literal: Mu Chong, a man of Dai—his ancestors for generations showed loyalty in the ages of Shenyuan and the Huan and Mu emperors.
idiomatic: Mu Chong came from Dai; his forebears had served loyally since the reigns of Emperor Shenyuan and the Huan and Mu emperors.

literal: In youth Chong took theft as his occupation.
idiomatic: In youth Chong lived by theft.

literal: When Daowu dwelt in the Dugu tribe Chong came and went supplying him—no one of the time could match it.
idiomatic: While Daowu stayed with the Dugu tribe Chong supplied him back and forth as no one else could.

literal: Later, in Liu Xian's rebellion, Emperor Pingwen's maternal grandson Liang Juan learned of it and secretly sent Chong to inform Daowu.
idiomatic: Later, when Liu Xian rebelled, Liang Juan—Emperor Pingwen's grandson by a daughter—learned of the plot and secretly sent Chong to warn Daowu.

literal: Juan told Chong, "If Xian learns of it, though swords cut and carve you, do not reveal it."
idiomatic: Juan told Chong, "If Xian finds out, let them cut you with swords—do not speak."

literal: He therefore gave Chong his favored wife and the fine horse he rode, saying, "If the matter is exposed, I shall use these to clear myself."
idiomatic: He gave Chong his favorite wife and his best horse, saying, "If we are found out, I will clear myself with these."

literal: Chong came to report the peril; Daowu galloped to the Helan tribe.
idiomatic: Chong brought word of danger; Daowu galloped to the Helan tribe.

literal: Xian indeed suspected Juan had leaked and was about to imprison him.
idiomatic: Xian indeed suspected Juan had leaked the plot and was about to seize him.

literal: Chong then proclaimed aloud, "Liang Juan has forgotten grace and righteousness and would make Xian rebel.
idiomatic: Chong then shouted aloud, "Liang Juan has forgotten grace and would make Xian rebel!

literal: Today I have seized his wife and horse—enough to settle the score."
idiomatic: I have taken his wife and horse—that settles the score."

literal: Xian heard and believed it.
idiomatic: Xian heard him and believed it.

literal: In the turmoil of Kudu, Chong's sister's son Yu Zhi and others with Chong plotted to seize Daowu in response.
idiomatic: During Kudu's revolt, Chong's nephew Yu Zhi and others plotted with Chong to seize Daowu in collusion.

literal: Chong by night informed Daowu; Daowu executed Zhi and the rest.
idiomatic: Chong warned Daowu by night; Daowu executed Zhi and his fellows.

literal: North across the Yin Mountains he again came to favor the Helan tribe.
idiomatic: He crossed the Yin Mountains to the north and again took refuge with the Helan tribe.

literal: Earlier, when Daowu fled Kudu's turmoil he sent Chong back to observe men's hearts.
idiomatic: Earlier, fleeing Kudu's revolt, Daowu had sent Chong back to gauge loyalties.

literal: Chong left his horse with attendants and in plain dress entered their camp.
idiomatic: Chong left his horse with attendants and entered the camp in disguise.

literal: There happened to be firelight; a pounding-woman recognized him and the bandits all sprang up in alarm.
idiomatic: Firelight betrayed him; a woman pounding grain recognized him and the rebels leapt up in alarm.

literal: Chong could not find his attendants; he hid in a pit, then slowly stole a horse and fled.
idiomatic: Unable to find his men, he hid in a pit, then slowly stole a horse and fled.

literal: He lodged in the great marsh; a white wolf came toward Chong and howled; Chong took warning, galloped after the wolf, and thus escaped peril.
idiomatic: He spent the night in a great marsh; a white wolf howled at him; taking it as a sign, he galloped after the wolf and escaped.

literal: Daowu marveled at it and ordered Chong to establish a shrine; descendants for generations have offered sacrifice.
idiomatic: Daowu marveled and ordered a shrine to Chong; descendants have sacrificed there ever since.

literal: In the Taihe era, recording meritorious subjects, Chong was granted joint sacrifice.
idiomatic: In the Taihe era, when meritorious subjects were recorded, Chong was granted joint sacrifice.

literal: Chong's eldest son Zhuliu, for merit, was granted Marquis of Lingling.
idiomatic: Chong's eldest son Zhuliu was enfeoffed Marquis of Lingling for merit.

literal: Later he was dismissed for crime.
idiomatic: He was later stripped of rank for a crime.

literal: His son Yi, for merit, was granted Duke of Fucheng.
idiomatic: His son Yi was enfeoffed Duke of Fucheng for merit.

literal: He died as Palace Attendant with posthumous title Jing.
idiomatic: He died as Palace Attendant with the posthumous title Jing.

literal: His son Zhen married the Princess of Changcheng and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
idiomatic: His son Zhen married the Princess of Changcheng and became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.

literal: Later an edict ordered divorce; he took the elder sister of the Civilized Empress.
idiomatic: Later an edict forced divorce; he married the Civilized Empress's elder sister.

literal: He held Southern Tribal Grand Chieftain, Palace Attendant, and died with posthumous title Xuan.
idiomatic: He served as Southern Tribal Grand Chieftain and Palace Attendant and died with the posthumous title Xuan.

literal: Xiaowen, recalling Chong's merit, ordered the Compiler Han Xianzong and Zhen together to fix the text of a stele and erect it on Mount Bai.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowen, remembering Chong's service, ordered Han Xianzong of the Compilation Bureau and Zhen to draft a stele and set it up on Mount Bai.

literal: Zhen's son Tai, original name Shiluo, was given his present name by Xiaowen.
idiomatic: Zhen's son Tai, originally named Shiluo, received his new name from Emperor Xiaowen.

literal: As a meritorious descendant he married the Princess of Zhangwu Chang and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law, in charge of the Four Bureaus of the Imperial Hunt.
idiomatic: As a meritorious scion he married the Princess of Zhangwu Chang, became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law, and oversaw the Four Bureaus of the Imperial Hunt.

literal: Later he was Right Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing and Marquis of Fufeng, then went out as Governor of Ding Province.
idiomatic: He later became Right Vice Minister of the Masters of Writing and Marquis of Fufeng, then went out as Governor of Ding Province.

literal: At first the Civilized Empress had confined Xiaowen in a separate chamber and was about to plot deposition and removal; Tai remonstrated sharply and she stopped.
idiomatic: When the Civilized Empress first confined Xiaowen apart and plotted to depose him, Tai remonstrated fiercely and she desisted.

literal: Xiaowen was grateful for his virtue and therefore favored him to the utmost.
idiomatic: Xiaowen owed him gratitude and favored him accordingly.

literal: He himself reported long illness and begged for Heng Province; it was granted.
idiomatic: He pleaded chronic illness and asked for Heng Province; the request was granted.

literal: Tai did not wish to move the capital and secretly plotted rebellion; with the Governor of Ding Province Lu Rui and the Marquis of Anle Yuan Long and others he plotted to set up the Prince of Yangping, Yi, of Shuozhou, as ruler.
idiomatic: Unwilling to see the capital moved, Tai secretly plotted rebellion with Lu Rui, governor of Ding Province, Yuan Long, Marquis of Anle, and others to make Yi, Prince of Yangping in Shuozhou, their sovereign.

literal: Yi secretly memorialized the matter; the emperor then sent the Prince of Rencheng, Cheng, to raise Bing and Si troops to attack them.
idiomatic: Yi reported them in a secret memorial; the emperor sent Prince Cheng of Rencheng with troops from Bing and Si to suppress them.

literal: Cheng first sent the Palace Writing Attendant Li Huan alone on horseback into Dai, taking them unawares.
idiomatic: Cheng first sent Li Huan of the Palace Writing Bureau alone on horseback into Dai to catch them off guard.

literal: Tai and the rest were alarmed and had no plan.
idiomatic: Tai and his party were thrown into panic with no plan left.

literal: Huan enlightened the rebels with gain and loss, showing fortune and calamity; the wicked party lost heart and none would serve them.
idiomatic: Huan explained fortune and ruin to the rebels; the plotters lost heart and none would fight for them.

literal: Tai judged he must fail and led his followers to attack Huan at the outer gate but could not take it.
idiomatic: Seeing defeat inevitable, Tai led his men against Huan at the outer gate and failed.

literal: He went out and was seized and sent in.
idiomatic: He fled, was captured, and sent to the capital.

literal: Xiaowen came to Dai; Tai and the rest were executed.
idiomatic: Xiaowen came to Dai; Tai and his fellows were executed.

literal: His son Shiru, style name Shuxian, was moved to Liang Province.
idiomatic: His son Shiru, styled Shuxian, was relocated to Liang Province.

literal: Later he was able to return and was made aide to the Grand Commandant.
idiomatic: He later returned and served as aide to the Grand Commandant.

literal: His son Zirong in youth loved learning and viewed nothing without reading.
idiomatic: His son Zirong loved learning from youth and read whatever he could find.

literal: He sought books from all under Heaven; whenever he met one he copied it, obtaining more than ten thousand scrolls.
idiomatic: He sought books across the realm, copying every text he found until he had more than ten thousand scrolls.

literal: Late in Wei he was concurrently Regular Attendant and envoy to Liang.
idiomatic: Late in Wei he served concurrently as Regular Attendant on an embassy to Liang.

literal: When Qi received the mandate he died as Minister of the Imperial Granaries.
idiomatic: When Qi took the mandate he died as Minister of the Imperial Granaries.

literal: Zhuliu's younger brother Guan, style name Tabo, inherited Chong's title.
idiomatic: Zhuliu's younger brother Guan, styled Tabo, inherited Chong's title.

literal: In youth he was famed for literary accomplishment.
idiomatic: In youth he was known for literary talent.

literal: In Mingyuan's time he was Left General of the Guard, managed the Gate and Secretariat, issued edicts, and inquired into old affairs—never was anything lost.
idiomatic: Under Emperor Mingyuan he was Left General of the Guard, oversaw the Gate and Secretariat, issued edicts, and traced precedents without ever losing a detail.

literal: He married the Princess of Yiyang and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law and Grand Commandant.
idiomatic: He married the Princess of Yiyang, became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law, and rose to Grand Commandant.

literal: When Taiwu supervised the state Guan was right-hand aide; going out he commanded the court, coming in he answered at the emperor's side—nothing great or small did not pass through his decision.
idiomatic: While Taiwu supervised the realm Guan was his right-hand man: abroad he directed government, at court he answered the heir—nothing large or small escaped his judgment.

literal: All day he was cheerful, without anger on his face.
idiomatic: He remained cheerful all day, never showing anger.

literal: He toiled, was modest, and skillfully guided others, not arrogant because of wealth and rank.
idiomatic: He worked hard, stayed modest, and guided others well, never arrogant in wealth or rank.

literal: In the eighth year of Taichang he died suddenly of illness, age thirty-five.
idiomatic: In the eighth year of Taichang he died suddenly of illness at thirty-five.

literal: Mingyuan came in person to his funeral and grieved so that those beside him were moved.
idiomatic: Mingyuan attended his funeral in person and grieved until those around him wept.

literal: He was granted a coffin of gold with hidden relief over the whole body; funeral rites followed entirely the precedent of the Prince of Ancheng, Shu Sun Jun.
idiomatic: He was given a coffin of gold with relief over the whole body; rites followed the precedent of Prince Shu Sun Jun of Ancheng.

literal: He was posthumously made Prince of Yidu with posthumous title Wencheng.
idiomatic: He was posthumously made Prince of Yidu with the title Wencheng.

literal: When Taiwu took the throne, whenever he talked and feasted with the ministers he never failed to sigh with earnest praise, thinking that since Daowu there had been no founding minister combining civil and military like him.
idiomatic: After Taiwu took the throne he never feasted with his ministers without sighing in praise, saying that since Daowu no founding minister had matched Guan's civil and military gifts.

literal: His son Shou inherited the title, married the Princess of Leling, and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
idiomatic: His son Shou inherited the title, married the Princess of Leling, and became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.

literal: Bright and keen, he had his father's manner.
idiomatic: Clever and sharp, he had his father's bearing.

literal: Taiwu loved and valued him and promoted him to Lower Grand Master.
idiomatic: Taiwu cherished him and promoted him to Lower Grand Master.

literal: In memorials and debate he was quick and had a voice within and without the court.
idiomatic: His memorials and debate were nimble, and his reputation rang inside and outside the court.

literal: He was transferred to Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and Southern Tribal Grand Chieftain, advanced to Prince of Yidu, and added General Who Pacifies the East.
idiomatic: He became Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and Southern Tribal Grand Chieftain, was advanced to Prince of Yidu, and named General Who Pacifies the East.

literal: Shou declined, saying, "My grandfather Chong, in the former emperor's age, often met hardship and peril.
idiomatic: Shou declined, saying, "My grandfather Chong, in the former emperor's day, met danger again and again.

literal: Fortune favored Liang Juan's sincere early warning, and so he could build merit for the former court and leave blessing for those after.
idiomatic: Heaven favored Liang Juan's loyal warning, so he served the earlier reign and left blessing for later generations.

literal: In antiquity Chen Ping received reward yet attributed the merit to one without knowledge.
idiomatic: In antiquity Chen Ping took reward yet credited one who knew nothing.

literal: Now Juan's founding merit is unrecorded while I alone through generations receive glory—is this not to look up ashamed before the ancient worthies and also to harm the state's statutes?"
idiomatic: Yet Juan's founding service goes unrecorded while I alone inherit glory age after age—should I not blush before the ancients and breach the state's law?"

literal: Taiwu praised this and then sought Juan's grandson and granted him a commandery duke.
idiomatic: Taiwu praised him, sought out Juan's grandson, and enfeoffed him Duke of a commandery.

literal: When the imperial carriage campaigned on Liang Province he ordered Shou to assist Jingmu and oversee all secrets; within and without all obeyed him.
idiomatic: On the Liangzhou campaign the emperor ordered Shou to assist Jingmu and control all confidential affairs; the whole court obeyed him.

literal: Halting at Yunzhong, about to cross the river, the emperor separately took the quiet chamber and summoned Shou, the Minister of Education Cui Hao, and the Master of Writing Li Shun, telling Shou, "Rouran's Wuti has joined with Mujian in alliance; now hearing that I campaign on Liangzhou he is sure to come violate the border.
idiomatic: At Yunzhong, before crossing the river, the emperor withdrew to a quiet room and summoned Shou, Minister Cui Hao, and Li Shun of the Masters of Writing, telling Shou, "Wuti of the Rouran has allied with Mujian; hearing that I march on Liangzhou he will surely raid the frontier.

literal: If we set ambush south of the desert, destroying them will be easy.
idiomatic: Ambush him south of the desert and destruction will be easy.

literal: When the pasturelands are finished, you may divide forces and lie in wait at critical points for the barbarians to arrive;
idiomatic: When the pastures are grazed out, post detachments at the key passes and wait for the enemy;

literal: draw them deep in, then strike.
idiomatic: lure them deep, then strike.

literal: If you disobey my command and the barbarians harm us, on my return I shall behead you.
idiomatic: Disobey my orders and let the barbarians harm the realm—I will behead you on my return.

literal: Cui Hao and Li Shun are witnesses—this is no empty word."
idiomatic: Hao and Shun are witnesses; this is no idle threat."

literal: Shou trusted the diviners' words that the enemy would not come and in the end made no preparations.
idiomatic: Shou trusted diviners who said the enemy would not come and made no preparations.

literal: Wuti indeed arrived and the capital was greatly alarmed.
idiomatic: Wuti came as foretold and the capital was thrown into terror.

literal: Shou did not know what to do and wished to build the western gate and ask Jingmu to avoid holding Mount Hui on the south for protection; the Empress Huibao would not listen and he stopped.
idiomatic: Shou knew not what to do, proposed sealing the western gate, and asked Jingmu to hold Mount Hui in the south; Empress Huibao refused and he desisted.

literal: He sent the Minister of Works Changsun Daosheng and others to attack them.
idiomatic: He sent Minister of Works Changsun Daosheng and others against them.

literal: When Taiwu returned, because there was no great harm he did not pursue blame.
idiomatic: Taiwu returned; as damage was slight he did not punish him.

literal: When Jingmu supervised the state Shou with Cui Hao and others assisted in government.
idiomatic: When Jingmu supervised the realm Shou assisted government with Cui Hao and others.

literal: All respected Hao, but Shou alone towered over him.
idiomatic: All honored Hao, but Shou alone looked down on him.

literal: He also relied on his position and office, thinking no one could match him.
idiomatic: He also trusted in rank and office, believing none could equal him.

literal: He told his son Shi, "Just let my son and me suffice to surpass others—there is no need to teach him painfully."
idiomatic: He told his son Shi, "Let my son and me alone surpass others—no need to drill him hard."

literal: Toward his uncles and brothers he was like toward slaves; husband and wife sat and ate together while he made his uncles eat leftovers.
idiomatic: He treated uncles and brothers like slaves; he and his wife ate together while making uncles take their leftovers.

literal: People of the time mocked him.
idiomatic: Contemporaries mocked him for it.

literal: On his death he was posthumously made Grand Commandant with posthumous title Wenzuan.
idiomatic: He died and was posthumously named Grand Commandant with the title Wenzuan.

literal: His son Pingguo inherited the title, married the Princess of Chengyang, and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law, Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and one of the crown prince's four tutors.
idiomatic: His son Pingguo inherited the title, married the Princess of Chengyang, and became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law, Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and one of the crown prince's four tutors.

literal: He died.
idiomatic: He died.

literal: His son Fugan inherited, married the Princess of Jibei, and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.
idiomatic: His son Fugan inherited, married the Princess of Jibei, and became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law.

literal: On his death his posthumous title was Kang.
idiomatic: He died with the posthumous title Kang.

literal: He had no son.
idiomatic: He left no son.

literal: Fugan's younger brother Pi inherited the title, married the Princess of Xinping, and was made Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law and garrison general of Wulao.
idiomatic: Fugan's younger brother Pi inherited the title, married the Princess of Xinping, and became Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law and garrison general of Wulao.

literal: Repeatedly he offended through lesser law; Xiaowen, because of his old merit and virtue, reproved him and pardoned him.
idiomatic: He repeatedly broke lesser statutes; Emperor Xiaowen, remembering old service, rebuked him and pardoned him each time.
